title: Transient Monocular Vision Loss (TMVL)
summary: TMVL is a critical neuro-ophthalmic emergency often serving as a 'warning shot' for impending stroke or permanent retinal infarction. This guide provides a comprehensive framework for the diagnosis, workup, and evidence-based management of amaurosis fugax.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: Transient Monocular Vision Loss (TMVL), traditionally termed 'Amaurosis Fugax,' is a sudden, temporary deficit in vision in one eye, typically lasting seconds to minutes, with complete recovery. It represents a Transient Ischemic Attack (TIA) of the retina, optic nerve, or choroid and demands immediate systemic investigation to prevent cerebrovascular accidents (CVA).

sections.title: The GCA Red Flag Screen
content: New onset headache or scalp tenderness
Jaw claudication (highest predictive value)
Anorexia, weight loss, or night sweats
Proximal muscle aches (Polymyalgia Rheumatica)
Afferent Pupillary Defect (APD) with pale disc edema
Elevated ESR (>50 mm/hr), CRP, and Platelets

sections.title: Diagnostic Investigation Workup
content: Step 1: Detailed History (Onset, duration, 'curtain' vs 'fog', triggers)
Step 2: Dilated Fundoscopy & BP measurement (urgent)
Step 3: Carotid Imaging (Duplex Ultrasound vs. CTA/MRA)
Step 4: Cardiac Workup (ECG, Holter monitor, Echocardiogram)
Step 5: Serology (CBC, PT/PTT, Lipid profile, A1c, ESR/CRP)
Step 6: Brain Imaging (MRI with DWI to rule out silent infarcts)

rows: Orbital tumors (cavernous hemangioma), Optic nerve sheath meningioma
Delayed photoreceptor recovery due to hypoperfusion
CEA beneficial (moderate reduction in stroke risk)

sections.title: Evidence-Based Medical Therapy
content: Antiplatelet Therapy: Aspirin (81-325mg) or Clopidogrel (Plavix) 75mg daily.
Dual Antiplatelet Therapy (DAPT): Often used for first 21-90 days post-symptom in high-risk patients.
High-Intensity Statins: Atorvastatin 80mg regardless of baseline LDL (SPARCL trial).
Blood Pressure Control: Target <130/80 mmHg (avoid aggressive drops in acute OIS).
Smoking Cessation: Essential to prevent plaque progression and rupture.

content.explanation: F: Flow (Carotid/Hemodynamic); U: Unusual (Vasospasm/Migraine); G: Giant Cell Arteritis (Must exclude!); A: Arrhythmia (Afib/Cardiac emboli); X: X-plore Hematological (Hypercoagulability).

sections.title: Ocular Ischemic Syndrome (OIS)
content: Caused by severe (>90%) carotid occlusion.
Mid-peripheral 'blossom' hemorrhages (dot-and-blot).
Dilated, non-tortuous retinal veins (distinct from CRVO).
Iridocyclitis & Neovascularization of the Iris (NVI).
Ocular Angina: Dull periocular ache from ischemia.

sections.title: Recent Advances: Landmark Studies
sections.content: The **POINT** and **CHANCE** trials have revolutionized early TIA management, showing that short-term DAPT (Aspirin + Clopidogrel) significantly reduces early recurrent stroke risk compared to aspirin alone. In the ophthalmic world, OCT-Angiography is emerging as a non-invasive tool to detect focal areas of capillary non-perfusion in post-TMVL patients.

sections.title: Surgical Techniques: CEA vs. CAS
content: CEA (Carotid Endarterectomy): Gold standard for most surgical candidates; removes the plaque directly.
CAS (Carotid Artery Stenting): Preferred in high-risk surgical anatomy (previous neck radiation, recurrent stenosis).
Crest Trial: Showed parity in outcomes between CEA and CAS for symptomatic patients in terms of stroke/death rates.

sections.title: Clinical Pearls for Resident Exams
content: TMVL in a young patient? Think Retinal Migraine, Cardiac Shunts (PFO), or Hypercoagulable states.
Bright light-induced amaurosis is pathognomonic for Ocular Ischemic Syndrome.
Always check for a carotid bruit, but remember: its absence does NOT rule out significant stenosis.
Venous stasis retinopathy (early OIS) is often mistaken for a mild CRVO; check the venous pulsation and tortuosity.
